elements.id-string-3: Nonparametric tests for functional data are a challenging class of tests to work with because of the potentially high dimensional nature of functional data.
elements.id-string-4: One of the main challenges for considering rank-based tests, like the Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests (MWW), is that the unit of observation is a curve.
elements.id-string-5: Thus any rank-based test must consider ways of ranking curves.
elements.id-string-6: While several procedures, including depth-based methods, have recently been used to create scores for rank-based tests, these scores are not constructed under the null and often introduce additional, uncontrolled for variability.
elements.id-string-7: We therefore reconsider the problem of rank-based tests for functional data and develop an alternative approach that incorporates the null hypothesis throughout.
elements.id-string-8: Our approach first ranks realizations from the curves at each time point, summarizes the ranks for each subject using a sufficient statistic we derive, and finally re-ranks the sufficient statistics in a procedure we refer to as a doubly ranked test.
elements.id-string-9: As we demonstrate, doubly rank tests are more powerful while maintaining ideal type I error in the two sample, MWW setting.
elements.id-string-10: We also extend our framework to more than two samples, developing a Kruskal-Wallis test for functional data which exhibits good test characteristics as well.
elements.id-string-11: Finally, we illustrate the use of doubly ranked tests in functional data contexts from material science, climatology, and public health policy.

elements.id-string-19: Depth is a popular and useful concept for ranking functions and many authors have utilized depth for Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon (MWW) type tests \citep{Lopez2009,Lopez2010,Lopez2017}, functional boxplots \citep{Sun2011, Genton2014, Wrobel2016}, outlier detection \citep{SunGenton2012, Dai2018, Huang2019, Dai2020, AlemanGomez2022}, and ranking curves \citep{Lopez2009, Lopez2011, Sun2012, Sguera2021}.
elements.id-string-20: The basic idea behind depth is to characterize the proportion of time a curve is bounded above and below by another curve in the sample.
elements.id-string-21: The resulting scores, when ordered, rank the curves from the inside out with the smallest values representing the extremes, the maximum or minimum, and the largest value representing the median \citep{Lopez2009, Sun2012}.

elements.id-string-300: In this manuscript, we investigate two novel nonparametric tests for comparing groups of functional curves: the doubly ranked MWW test and the doubly ranked KW test.
elements.id-string-301: The tests arise from the same sufficient statistic derived using the distribution of the ranks under $H_0$ over time.
elements.id-string-302: Treating the ranks from individual curves as a sample over time and using a sufficient statistic to summarize that sample allows us to reduce the dimensionality of the testing problem and improve efficiency.
elements.id-string-303: While other approaches reduce dimensionality using a summary score for the data, only ours uses a score that is built under $H_0$.
elements.id-string-304: Doubly ranked tests are distribution free, relying on the rank of the geometric means of the ranks over time.
elements.id-string-305: We demonstrate empirically that our doubly ranked MWW performs well in terms of type I error and power for a variety of true error distributions.
elements.id-string-306: While some power is lost as the underlying correlation in the curves increases, we see gains in power as both $n$ and $S$ increase.
elements.id-string-307: These results hold up in the doubly ranked KW test as well.
elements.id-string-308: The test procedures we propose here are global tests of differences between curves, as are the other methods by \cite{Hall2007,Lopez2009,Lopez2010,Chak2015} and \cite{Melendez2021}.
elements.id-string-309: With any global test, one must be careful to examine the underlying data for where the differences lie.
elements.id-string-310: These tests can instruct us that there is difference but can't be used to identify exactly where the difference is nor can they tell us the magnitude of difference.
elements.id-string-311: For that, we would need to model the group location curves themselves and rely on point-wise testing, ideally adjusted for multiple testing.
elements.id-string-312: See, for example, some of the work on functional regression reviewed in \cite{Morris2015} and \cite{Greven2017}.
elements.id-string-313: Point-wise testing is not goal of this work, however our method can be useful as a global test in a variety of data contexts.
elements.id-string-314: In our data illustrations, we demonstrate the use of the doubly ranked MWW and KW tests to study problems in material science, climatology, and public health policy.
elements.id-string-315: Specifically, we show the doubly ranked tests can detect differences in groups of curves defined by conditions in a resin viscosity experiment, identify differences in temperature and precipitation across Canadian regions, and find differences in population mobility in the surrounding COVID-19 policy implementations.
elements.id-string-316: The tests can be performed as a main analysis or a first pass analysis in conjunction with other modeling steps.
elements.id-string-317: Our tests are also easy to implement and easy for practitioners to interpret---in particular, for those who are already familiar with univariate MWW and KW tests.
elements.id-string-318: Doubly ranked testing is not limited to functional data applications nor is it even limited to FACE-based preprocessed data.
elements.id-string-319: The assumptions for the tests apply broadly to both functional and multivariate data.
